keyAndScale.primaryKey: F major, built entirely on power chords with no clear major/minor distinction due to the absence of thirds

scalesUsed.application: Brief guitar solo uses major pentatonic fragments; the bright, raw character fits the aggressive delivery
Blues-rock bends in the solo section; mixing major and minor pentatonic creates the raw garage rock edge

keyAndScale.modalCharacter: Ambiguous major/minor due to exclusive use of power chords (no thirds); the raw, distorted tone creates a proto-punk atmosphere
keyAndScale.keySignature: 1 flat (Bb) nominally, but the power chord approach makes traditional key signatures less relevant
keyAndScale.relativeMinor: D minor is the relative minor of F major

mainProgression.description: The entire song is built on just two power chords a whole step apart - F5 and G5. This primal simplicity, played with Dave Davies' slashed-speaker distortion, launched the power chord as the fundamental unit of rock guitar.

sectionProgressions.description: The relentless two-chord riff that drives the entire song, played with aggressive eighth-note strumming and raw distortion
The same two-chord pattern shifted up a whole step for the 'You really got me' refrain, creating a simple but effective lift
Brief descending power chord line used as a turnaround, resolving back to the F5 root

harmonicFunction: F5 (I) - Tonic power chord, the driving home base of the song
G5 (II) - Supertonic power chord creating the signature push-pull tension with F5
A5 (III) - Mediant power chord, same interval relationship shifted up for the chorus elevation
C5 (V) - Dominant power chord used briefly in turnarounds
Bb5 (IV) - Subdominant power chord in the descending turnaround figure

techniques.name: Two-Chord Power Chord Riff
techniques.description: The foundational power chord riff alternating between F5 and G5 with aggressive downstroke strumming and raw distortion - the riff that invented hard rock guitar

notes: F5: 1-3-3-X-X-X (barre power chord at 1st fret)
G5: 3-5-5-X-X-X (barre power chord at 3rd fret)
The riff is a rapid alternation between these two shapes
Dave Davies achieved the distorted tone by slashing his speaker cone with a razor blade
Use heavy downstrokes with a loose, aggressive strumming hand
sequence: Fret the F5 power chord at the 1st fret (index bars, ring and pinky on 3rd fret)
Strike with aggressive downstrokes in eighth-note rhythm
Slide up two frets to G5 at the 3rd fret
Continue the same strumming pattern on G5
Alternate back and forth maintaining the driving rhythm
tips: The power chord shape stays exactly the same - only the position shifts
Keep your fretting hand in the power chord shape and slide as a unit
The tone should be raw and aggressive - embrace a slightly messy, garage sound
All downstrokes give the riff its characteristic pounding energy
Mute the top three strings with the underside of your index finger

techniques.name: Power Chord Shifting (Chorus Lift)
techniques.description: Shifting the same two-chord pattern up a whole step to G5-A5 for the chorus, creating a simple harmonic lift using identical technique at a new position

notes: G5: 3-5-5-X-X-X (barre power chord at 3rd fret)
A5: 5-7-7-X-X-X (barre power chord at 5th fret)
Same power chord shape and strumming pattern as the verse
The shift up creates an instant energy boost for the chorus
The technique is identical - only the fret position changes
sequence: At the chorus, shift the F5-G5 pattern up to G5-A5
Maintain the same aggressive eighth-note strumming
The G5 now becomes the lower chord, A5 the upper
After the chorus, shift back down to F5-G5 for the verse
The turnaround uses C5-Bb5-F5 to return to the home key
tips: The beauty of power chords is that the shape never changes
Practice sliding the shape cleanly between positions without losing rhythm
The chorus should feel like a natural escalation, not a jarring change
Keep your thumb behind the neck for smooth positional shifts

techniques.name: Aggressive Downstroke Rhythm
techniques.description: The relentless all-downstroke eighth-note strumming technique that gives the song its primal, driving energy - the foundation of punk guitar playing

notes: Every strum is a downstroke - no upstrokes in the rhythm part
Eighth notes at 140 BPM means 280 downstrokes per minute
The strumming arm should stay loose to avoid fatigue
Strumming comes from the wrist, not the elbow
This technique directly influenced the Ramones and punk guitar style
sequence: Lock your picking hand into a steady eighth-note pattern
Strike only on downstrokes, returning the hand quickly for the next stroke
Keep the motion compact and efficient from the wrist
Maintain absolute rhythmic consistency throughout the song
Do not slow down or speed up - the relentless tempo is essential
tips: If your forearm starts cramping, you are strumming from the elbow - use the wrist
Practice the downstroke pattern on open strings before adding chords
Start at 100 BPM and build up to 140 BPM gradually
The tone should be aggressive but not sloppy - each stroke should be clear
This is a stamina exercise - build endurance over daily practice sessions

sections.name: Intro / Main Riff
sections.description: The riff that launched hard rock - F5 to G5 power chords with raw, speaker-shredding distortion that changed guitar forever
notes: Aggressive downstrokes on the power chords at 140 BPM
The distorted tone is essential to the sound - clean tone loses the character
The riff should feel primal and driving
This two-chord pattern continues virtually unchanged through the entire song

sections.name: Verse
sections.description: Same F5-G5 riff continues under the verse vocals, the relentless two-chord engine driving Ray Davies' urgent vocal delivery
notes: The riff does not change for the verse - same relentless energy
Vocal melody rides on top of the unchanging power chord rhythm
Keep the strumming intensity consistent, no dynamic dips
The simplicity is the point - do not try to add variations

sections.name: Chorus
sections.description: the signature refrain shifts up to G5-A5, creating an instant lift of energy with the same two-chord approach at a higher position
notes: Same riff pattern shifted up a whole step for the chorus
The positional shift creates a natural energy boost
The strumming intensity can increase slightly here
Brief C5-Bb5-F5 turnaround to return to the verse

sections.name: Guitar Solo
sections.description: Dave Davies' raw, distorted guitar solo over the F5-G5 riff pattern, using pentatonic licks with the same aggressive attitude as the rhythm
notes: Solo uses F minor/major pentatonic at the 1st position
Raw, aggressive bends and hammer-ons matching the song's energy
The rhythm guitar continues the F5-G5 riff underneath
The solo is short and explosive, matching the song's brevity

sections.name: Outro
sections.description: Final verse and chorus repetitions driving to the abrupt ending, the song burning out as fast as it exploded to life
sections.progression: F5 - G5 riff into G5 - A5 chorus, ending on F5
notes: Final repetitions of verse and chorus patterns
Maximum intensity throughout the outro
The song ends abruptly on the F5 - no fade-out, just a hard stop
The entire song is over in 2:14 - do not overstay the welcome

guitar.recommended: Any electric guitar with a humbucker or hot single-coil pickup
alternatives: Gibson Les Paul Junior (single P-90 pickup)
Any guitar that can handle distortion without excessive feedback
guitar.pickup: Bridge pickup for maximum aggression and bite; Dave Davies used an Elpico amplifier with a slashed speaker

amp.recommended: Small tube amp cranked to maximum for natural speaker breakup
alternatives: Any small tube amp pushed to its limits
A fuzz or distortion pedal into a clean amp for the modern equivalent

settings.gain: 8-10 (maximum overdrive - this song demands a cranked, ragged tone)

effects.distortion: The original tone came from Dave Davies literally slashing his speaker cone with a razor blade. A heavy fuzz pedal (like a Maestro FZ-1 or EHX Big Muff) or cranked small amp gives the closest modern equivalent.
effects.other: No effects needed. The rawness is the point. A fuzz pedal is the only consideration for modern players.

beginner.focus: Learn the two-chord power chord riff - this is one of the simplest and most important riffs in rock history
steps: Learn the F5 power chord shape at the 1st fret
Learn the G5 power chord shape at the 3rd fret
Practice sliding between F5 and G5 while maintaining strumming rhythm
Play the riff at slow tempo, building up to 140 BPM

intermediate.focus: Master the full song structure with the chorus shift and turnaround
steps: Add the chorus shift to G5-A5 at the 3rd and 5th frets
Practice the all-downstroke stamina at full 140 BPM tempo
Play through the complete 2:14 song without stopping

advanced.focus: Learn the guitar solo and dial in the authentic raw distortion tone
steps: Learn the F pentatonic solo licks at the 1st position
Practice aggressive bends and hammer-ons for the solo
Experiment with fuzz pedals to find the slashed-speaker tone
Play the complete song including solo with authentic feel and attitude

commonMistakes: Playing too cleanly - this song requires raw, aggressive distortion to sound right
Adding unnecessary chord variations - the beauty is in the two-chord simplicity
Using alternate picking instead of all downstrokes, which loses the driving energy
Playing too slowly - the 140 BPM tempo is essential to the urgent, explosive feel
practiceRoutine: Practice the F5-G5 power chord slide with a metronome for 3 minutes
Build downstroke stamina with steady eighth notes on F5 at gradually increasing tempo (5 minutes)
Practice the verse-to-chorus position shift from F5-G5 to G5-A5 (3 minutes)
Run through the complete song at tempo (3 minutes)
Cool down with slow power chord slides for clean technique (2 minutes)
focusAreas: Clean power chord slides between positions (no buzzing during transitions)
Consistent strumming intensity throughout the song
Proper string muting on top three strings to avoid unwanted noise
metronomeWork: Start the F5-G5 riff at 100 BPM with all downstrokes
Increase by 10 BPM every few minutes until reaching 140 BPM
Practice holding the tempo steady for the full 2:14 duration without drift
The fast tempo requires wrist-based strumming - monitor for elbow tension
